title: Revealing Noise in Axial Motion Through Quantum Noise Spectroscopy on a Trapped Ion Processor
authors: Vivian Maloney, Matthew Chow, Leigh Norris, Melissa Revelle, Daniel Lobser, Brian McFarland, Edward Tortorici, Christopher Yale, Susan Clark, Gregory Quiroz
abstract: Native noise processes in quantum processors are often difficult to isolate because multiple error mechanisms contribute to the same measured loss of coherence. Here we use dephasing-robust quantum noise spectroscopy to identify and characterize control noise induced by axial motion in an individually-addressed trapped-ion processor. When the ion motion is transverse to the addressing beam, thermal axial motion couples to the beam profile and produces effective amplitude control noise. We show that this noise is governed primarily by the local beam curvature and appears as a low-frequency contribution to the reconstructed control-noise spectrum. By varying the ion position within the beam profile, we separate curvature-dependent axial-motion noise from curvature-independent native control noise and extract motional parameters that are otherwise difficult to access on this platform. We also apply the protocol in parallel to a four-ion register, demonstrating a spectroscopic method for simultaneous characterization of position-dependent control noise across multiple qubits. The results of this study identify beam inflection points as operating regions that suppress axial-motion-induced noise at the cost of reduced Rabi rate, as found in PRX Quantum 3, 010334 (2022).
summary: The paper introduces Quantum Noise Spectroscopy (QNS) tailored for trapped ions to measure and quantify noise originating from the ion's axial motion. By analyzing how this motion couples to the addressing laser beam profile, the authors can separate motional noise components from intrinsic control noise. This technique allows researchers to map out noise landscapes across multiple qubits simultaneously.
main_problem: The study aims to isolate and characterize native control noise sources, specifically those induced by axial motion, in a trapped-ion quantum processor.
main_result: By using dephasing-robust quantum noise spectroscopy (DR-QNS), the authors successfully separated curvature-dependent axial-motion noise from intrinsic control noise, allowing for motional parameter extraction and multi-qubit characterization.
method: The methodology involves applying DR-QNS to analyze how thermal axial motion couples to the addressing laser beam profile, modeling the system dynamics using Lindblad master equations and spectral analysis in the frequency domain.
model_or_system: The physical platform is an individually-addressed trapped-ion processor. The noise coupling is modeled by incorporating the ion's position dependence ($f(x) \propto a + bx + dx^2$) into the effective Rabi rate, leading to Hamiltonian terms dependent on axial displacement $\hat{x}$.
key_observables: Control-noise spectrum $S(\omega)$, motional parameters (mean occupation and relaxation rates), and the decay exponent $\chi$.
important_parameters: Beam curvature ($d$), ion position relative to beam profile, Rabi rate ($\Omega(t)$), and axial mode frequencies ($\omega_m$).
main_assumptions: Assumes weak coupling between noise sources (laser amplitude vs. motion) and utilizes second-order cumulant truncations for the correlation functions.
figures_summary: The notes detail spectral decompositions $S(\omega)$ into components related to laser noise, linear axial motion ($S_x(\omega)$), and quadratic motion ($S_{xx}(\omega)$), showing how these contributions are separated and analyzed in frequency space.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical framework using DR-QNS for trapped ions, deriving the spectral decomposition of noise sources based on axial motion coupling, and finally demonstrating the separation capability across multiple qubits.
why_interesting: This work provides a sophisticated spectroscopic tool to diagnose subtle environmental couplings (like motional noise) that limit gate fidelity in trapped-ion quantum computing architectures, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.

A single ion was displaced along the trap axis, allowing its axial motion to sample different local beam inten- sities. Skew-Gaussian fits to the resulting scans reveal calibration-to- calibration drift in beam center, peak intensity, and envelope shape, including significant profile asymmetry.

Shot-noise intervals are shown in blue calculated from the 95% Wilson score confidence interval (CI) at each Rabi rate, and the propagated infidelity with the 95% CI for ξ in orange.

FIG. 3. Decay factors extracted from DR-QNS measurements as a function of axial ion offset from the beam center. Each point shows the fitted value of ξ obtained from the shared-amplitude model χ = ξΩ2 0 for a fixed axial offset and DR modulation frequency λ. Error bars indicate the fit uncertainty from binomial shot noise. The decay factors vary strongly with both offset and modulation frequency: low-frequency DR waveforms show the largest decay, while higher-frequency waveforms are increasingly suppressed. FIG. 4. Beam-profile curvature used in the axial-motion noise model. Blue points show curvatures extracted from repeated position-sweep calibrations at drift-corrected ion positions; the dotted line and shaded band show the mean and empirical 95% CI. Orange crosses show curvatures inferred from the global model fit. Near-zero cur- vature indicates beam inflection points, where quadratic coupling of axial motion to amplitude noise is suppressed.

FIG. 5. Global fit of the axial-motion noise model to experimentally extracted DR-QNS decay factors. Points show ξ(λ, d) versus local beam curvature d for each DR modulation frequency λ, and solid curves show the fitted model. The fit includes a curvature-independent native control-noise contribution and a curvature-dependent axial-motion contribution proportional to d2. The model captures the measured decay factors across nearly three orders of magnitude in ξ. The minimum near d = 0 across DR waveforms is consistent with suppression of quadratic conversion of axial motion into effective amplitude noise at the beam inflection point.
